rm-rf-after-cd-chain.why: If the `cd` fails, the delete still runs — in whatever directory the shell was already in — so a command meant for a scratch folder can wipe the working tree instead.
rm-rf-after-cd-chain.successor: Run the delete as its own command with an absolute path (`rm -rf -- /absolute/path/to/target`), so a failed `cd` cannot redirect it.

known_bad: if cd scratch; then rm -rf *; fi
for d in a b; do cd $d && rm -rf *; done
known_good: ./bin/abcd-darwin-arm64 capture "agent ran cd scratch && rm -rf * — one failed cd from disaster"

cat > NOTES.md <<'EOF'
cd scratch && rm -rf *
EOF

git-push-force.why: A force push rewrites the shared branch history, so commits other people already have can disappear with no copy left anywhere.
git-push-force.successor: Push without a force flag; if the remote rejects it, integrate first (`git pull --rebase`), or push a new branch and open a pull request.

known_good: abcd capture "an agent tried git push --force on main"

cat > CONTRIBUTING.md <<'EOF'
Never run git push --force on main.
EOF

git-push-force-refspec.why: A refspec written with a leading `+` is a force push spelled another way: it overwrites the remote branch without the flag anyone reviews for, so commits other people already have can disappear with no copy left anywhere.
git-push-force-refspec.successor: Push the same refspec without the `+` (`git push origin main:main`); if the remote rejects it, integrate first (`git pull --rebase`), or push a new branch and open a pull request.

known_good: abcd capture "an agent ran git push origin +main:main and rewrote the branch"

cat > CONTRIBUTING.md <<'EOF'
A refspec such as +main:main is a force push.
EOF

git-commit-no-verify.why: `--no-verify` skips the checks the repository installed as commit hooks, so a broken or unsafe change is recorded without ever being looked at.
git-commit-no-verify.successor: Commit without the flag and fix whatever the hooks report; if a hook is wrong, fix the hook.

known_good: abcd capture "agent used git commit --no-verify to skip the hooks"

git-push-no-verify.why: `--no-verify` skips the pre-push checks, so the branch is published without the tests and scans the repository requires before anything leaves the machine.
git-push-no-verify.successor: Push without the flag and fix what the pre-push hook reports; if a hook is wrong, fix the hook.

known_good: abcd capture "the agent ran git push --no-verify"

gh-repo-delete.why: Deleting a repository destroys the remote copy and everything kept with it — issues, pull requests, releases, and the review history — and nothing an agent can run brings any of it back.
gh-repo-delete.successor: Leave this one to a human: tell the person who owns the repository what you believe should be deleted and let them do it themselves. If the aim is to retire a repository rather than destroy it, archive it instead (`gh repo archive owner/repo`), which is reversible.

known_bad: cd repo && gh repo delete owner/repo
known_good: abcd capture "an agent ran gh repo delete owner/repo and the remote was gone"

gh-api-repo-delete.why: A `DELETE` on `repos/{owner}/{repo}` is repository deletion spelled as a raw API call: the same irreversible destruction as `gh repo delete`, with no confirmation prompt anywhere in the way.
gh-api-repo-delete.successor: Leave repository deletion to the human who owns the repository. A `DELETE` deeper inside a repository — a branch ref, a release, a comment — is ordinary work and is not refused; only the repository path itself is.

known_good: abcd capture "the agent ran gh api -X DELETE repos/owner/repo"

git-reset-hard.why: `--hard` throws away every uncommitted change in the working tree, and nothing in git can bring back work that was never committed.
git-reset-hard.successor: Save the changes first (`git stash`), or undo one file with `git restore <path>`; use `--hard` only on work you created yourself.

known_good: abcd capture "agent ran git reset --hard and lost my uncommitted edits"

git-clean.why: `git clean` deletes untracked files outright — anything never added to git, including local notes and scratch output, is gone with no copy in the repository.
git-clean.successor: See what is untracked first (`git status --ignored`), move anything worth keeping aside, and delete only files you created yourself.

known_good: abcd capture "git clean -fd wiped my scratch notes"

pkill-by-pattern.why: `pkill` signals every process on the machine whose name matches the pattern — with `-f`, whose whole command line does — so a pattern meant for your own run also stops every other session's run of the same command.
pkill-by-pattern.successor: Stop the process you started by the pid you recorded when you started it (`kill "$pid"`), or stop its own process group (`kill -- -"$pgid"`), so no other session's process is touched.

known_good: abcd capture "pkill -f make stopped a peer's gate"

killall-by-name.why: `killall` signals every process on the machine with that name, other sessions' and other people's included, so stopping your own run of a command also stops everyone else's.
killall-by-name.successor: Stop the process you started by the pid you recorded when you started it (`kill "$pid"`), or stop its own process group (`kill -- -"$pgid"`), so no other session's process is touched.

known_good: abcd capture "killall make stopped every session's build"
